answer:
Yes—Paul Graham strongly recommends going to Silicon Valley, at least for a while. His April 2026 advice to Stockholm founders explicitly allows returning home. He does not mean that success in Stockholm is impossible or that you must emigrate permanently.

His main argument is about the people around you: a larger concentration of strong peers, useful chance encounters, faster decisions, and a culture of helping without immediately expecting something back. He thinks the biggest benefit is how that environment changes your ambition: meeting highly successful founders makes their achievements feel difficult but attainable.

He also sees fundraising advantages. In his view, competition pushes Valley investors to decide faster, and attracting interest there can make Swedish investors take you more seriously.

There are qualifications. He reports that YC companies returning home are about half as likely to become billion-dollar companies as those staying, but acknowledges selection bias and higher Bay Area valuations. That comparison does not establish that moving doubles your particular startup’s chances. He recommends YC as a concentrated route into the ecosystem, while acknowledging his interest as its co-founder. He also accepts that family can matter more than maximizing company value.

My practical recommendation, assuming you want a globally ambitious startup, is to test spending a sustained period there before committing permanently. Build alongside founders, meet prospective customers and investors, and assess whether access produces useful relationships and faster progress. Consider YC if it fits. Stay longer if the benefits justify the cost; return if Stockholm offers stronger customer access, team stability, or family support. Returning can also strengthen Stockholm’s startup community.
